titre: Twenty Years Before the Legend of Phineas Gage
accroche: In 1848, an iron bar passes through Phineas Gage's skull without killing him; the detailed portrait of his change of character appears twenty years later
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 13, 1848, around 4:30 p.m., near Cavendish, Vermont, Phineas Gage, twenty-five, a foreman on the Rutland and Burlington railroad work site, tamps a charge of powder into a blasting hole. The tamping iron strikes the rock, the powder explodes, and the bar, more than a meter long and weighing about six kilos, passes through his left cheek and his left frontal lobe, then exits at the top of his skull. Gage falls backward, has a few convulsions, then speaks within a few minutes. His workers carry him to an ox cart, where he sits upright for more than a kilometer to the village hotel.

## A Documented Recovery, a Character Described Late

The physician John M. Harlow treats him: foul discharge, fungus protruding from the brain, abscesses, then about ten days of semi-comatose state until early October. He improves, and walks on the stairs in November. In his December 1848 report, Harlow also notes that Gage misjudges sizes and sums of money, and that on October 20 he is “very childish.” He reserves the patient's mental manifestations for a later communication.

About a year after the accident, the Harvard surgeon Henry J. Bigelow, with whom Gage spends about two months, declares him completely recovered, physically and mentally (text of 1850).

The portrait that became influential dates from 1868. Harlow then publishes “Recovery from the Passage of an Iron Bar Through the Head” and describes in it Gage's state at his April 1849 visit: his former employers judge the change too marked to give him back his position, he is irreverent and capricious, “a child in his intellectual capacity and manifestations,” with “the animal passions of a strong man,” and his friends say he is “no longer Gage.” Harlow only picked up the family's trail in July 1866; it is from Gage's mother and brother-in-law that he learns what followed and the end.

## A Late Description Turned Textbook Case

According to the 2022 analysis that cites this text, this account, compiled twenty years after the accident, remains very general and, in many respects, vague. It has nonetheless become the reference: of twenty-five journal articles published between 1994 and 2020, excluding historical syntheses, 92% describe a personality change and 52% psychopath-like behavior, against only 16% that mention a recovery. Many cite Harlow without recalling that this evidence is circumstantial.

This recovery, however, appears in the same text by Harlow: in 1851, Gage works for almost a year and a half in a livery stable in Hanover, New Hampshire; from 1852 to 1860, he lives in Chile, where he looks after horses and drives a stagecoach pulled by six horses. Returned to his mother's home in San Francisco, he dies on May 21, 1861, according to Harlow, after convulsions that Harlow judges epileptic, twelve and a half years after the accident, according to Harlow and the Harvard catalog. The skull and the bar arrived at Harvard in 1868.

The injury is thus documented from the first weeks. The change of character is far less so: a late account, which Bigelow contradicts in 1850, and which is most often cited today without these reservations.

repere.texte: Of twenty-five journal articles published between 1994 and 2020 and analyzed in 2022, excluding historical syntheses, 92% describe a personality change in Gage and 52% psychopath-like behavior, against only 16% that mention his recovery.
repere.source: Schleim S., “Neuroscience Education Begins With Good Science: Communication About Phineas Gage (1823-1860)...,” Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 16:734174, 2022

carte.punch: Gage's “psychopath” portrait rests on a text published twenty years after his accident.
carte.idee: In 1848, an iron bar passes through Phineas Gage's skull without killing him. The portrait of a changed man rests mainly on a text by his physician published in 1868, judged vague in 2022, while Bigelow called him recovered in 1850. Gage then worked, and later drove a stagecoach in Chile.

quiz.question: Why does the image of Phineas Gage turned “psychopath” after his accident rest on fragile evidence?
choix: Because the physicians of the time had no vocabulary to describe a change in behavior
Because it rests mainly on an account published twenty years after the events, which the 2022 analysis judges general and vague
Because Gage's skull, now kept at Harvard, bears no trace of the injury
Because Gage died less than a year after his accident
quiz.explication: Harlow publishes this portrait in 1868, twenty years after the accident, and the 2022 analysis judges it very general and vague. The physicians of the time knew how to describe behavior (Harlow himself does), the skull kept at Harvard does bear the fracture, and Gage lived more than ten years after the accident.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the surgeon Henry Jacob Bigelow observe when he examines Gage about a year after the accident?
choix: A man completely recovered, physically and mentally
A complete blindness in both eyes
A total loss of speech, compensated by gestures
A man unable to walk without help
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bigelow, a surgeon at Harvard, declares Gage completely recovered, physically and mentally (text of 1850). Gage lost the sight of his left eye only, spoke, and Harlow describes in April 1849 a steady gait.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Phineas Gage do in the years following his accident, according to the sources documenting his recovery?
choix: He remains institutionalized, unable to work, until his death
He works with horses, then drives a stagecoach in Chile
He becomes a physician and himself publishes an account of his case
He regains his position as foreman on the railroad work site
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Harlow reports that in 1851 Gage works in a stable, then that he lives in Chile from 1852 to 1860, looking after horses and driving a six-horse stagecoach. His former employers, for their part, judged the change too marked to give him back his position.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 2022 analysis of twenty-five journal articles devoted to the Gage case, what proportion mention his recovery?
choix: More than nine in ten, or 92%
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of twenty-five articles analyzed, 92% describe a personality change and 52% psychopath-like behavior, but only 16%, or four articles, mention Gage's recovery.
